payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=Can+simulative+reasoning+frameworks+effectively+detect+reasoning+blind+spots+without+relying+on+pre-defined+evaluation+datasets%3F&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7304238\", \"title\": [\"Logical Equivalence, Metacognitive Interference, and Scoring Blind Spots in Inductive Reasoning Tests: On the Structural Invalidity of IQ Scores as a Measure of Reasoning Ability\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The test items used in IQ testing to measure fluid reasoning-whether number series or figural matrix reasoning-all rely on the same inductive reasoning structure: \\\"given finite samples, infer a rule, predict the next term.\\\" This paper identifies three structural problems with such items: (1) Logical equivalence: given any finite sequence or matrix, there often exist multiple generative rules that are computationally equivalent in their outputs, yet the test scores solely on output, making it impossible to distinguish the quality of reasoning paths; (2) Metacognitive interference: high-metacognitive test-takers automatically engage an \\\"auditing procedure\\\" (questioning the premise of the item, identifying multiple interpretations), which consumes working memory resources and induces response delays, resulting in systematic time-pressure penalties; (3) Skeptical disposition and deference to authority presuppositions: the standardized testing procedure implicitly demands that test-takers not question the items themselves, not question the testing institution, and not question the system which claims that intelligence can be measured by a single score. Test-takers with a habitual skeptical disposition automatically initiate the auditing procedure, consuming additional cognitive resources and thereby being systematically penalized in performance. Furthermore, practice effects allow test-takers to compress \\\"reasoning\\\" into \\\"pattern matching,\\\" thereby bypassing the auditing procedure and significantly improving scores-this further demonstrates that when practice becomes normative, what the test measures is no longer fluid reasoning but crystallized pattern recognition. This paper argues that IQ scores are not a pure indicator of \\\"fluid reasoning ability,\\\" but an inseparable hybrid of \\\"fluid reasoning ability,\\\" \\\"familiarity with the test format,\\\" and \\\"deference to authority presuppositions.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7304238\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/1-4020-4943-9_4\", \"title\": [\"Simulative Reasoning and Plan Recognition\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/1-4020-4943-9_4\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1080/13546783.2023.2189163\", \"title\": [\"Bullshit blind spots: the roles of miscalibration and information processing in bullshit detection\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1080/13546783.2023.2189163\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2023, 3, 14]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.54254/2755-2721/2026.37201\", \"title\": [\"An Empirical Investigation of Whether Role Asymmetry Can Overcome Reasoning Blind Spots in Homogeneous Models through Adaptive Routing and Local Repair\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Under the test-time compute scaling paradigm, improving the multi-step reasoning accuracy of lightweight large language models within a limited computational budget remains a critical challenge. Existing self-correction and multi-agent debate methods often suffer from rigid interaction schemes, coarse-grained correction, and homogeneous role configurations. Whether role-asymmetric constraints can enable a critic agent to overcome the reasoning biases of its generator has rarely been tested directly. This paper develops a collaborative reasoning framework combining adaptive routing with role-asymmetric local repair, treating this hypothesis as a falsifiable research question, and conducts systematic experiments on two backbone models, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B. Results show that the framework's disadvantage relative to simple baselines is capability-dependent: on the weaker model, it is statistically indistinguishable from standard chain-of-thought and other single-model baselines while significantly outperforming multi-agent debate; on the stronger model, it significantly underperforms most baselines. A sanity check confirms that the critic reliably identifies clearly structured arithmetic errors; however, its recall drops sharply on subtle errors requiring cross-step verification of quantitative relationships, and the net effect of repair mirrors this pattern, close to neutral on the weaker model and clearly negative on the stronger one. Ablation experiments show that the marginal effects of routing and role asymmetry reverse with model capability, turning negative on the stronger model even as removing either component improves its accuracy. These findings provide reproducible empirical evidence for systematic reasoning blind spots in self-criticism by homogeneous models, and indicate that role asymmetry implemented only through prompting cannot reliably overcome cognitive homogeneity.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.54254/2755-2721/2026.37201\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 9, 22]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "e3355155b59a711f233000bca6611e86418c165907d11e5e5142093f02d85979", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unrecognized_reasoning_limits", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7304238", "doi:10.1007/1-4020-4943-9_4", "doi:10.1080/13546783.2023.2189163", "doi:10.54254/2755-2721/2026.37201"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7304238", "https://doi.org/10.1007/1-4020-4943-9_4", "https://doi.org/10.1080/13546783.2023.2189163", "https://doi.org/10.54254/2755-2721/2026.37201"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

Abstract
Agreement Technologies refer to open computer systems in which autonomous
software agents interact with one another, typically on behalf of humans, in order
to come to mutually acceptable agreements. With the advance of AI systems in
recent years, it has become apparent that such agreements, in order to be accept-
able to the involved parties, must remain aligned with ethical principles and
moral values. However, this is notoriously difficult to ensure, especially as differ-
ent human users (and their software agents) may hold different value systems,
i.e. they may differently weigh the importance of individual moral values. Fur-
thermore, it is often hard to specify the precise meaning of a value in a particular
context in a computational manner. Methods to estimate value systems based
on human-engineered specifications, e.g. based on value surveys, are limited in
scale due to the need for intense human moderation. In this article, we propose a
novel method to automaticallylearnvalue systems from observations and human
demonstrations. In particular, we propose a formal model of thevalue system
learningproblem, its instantiation to sequential decision-making domains based
on multi-objective Markov decision processes, as well as tailored preference-based
and inverse reinforcement learning algorithms to infer value grounding functions

1 Introduction
Agreement Technologies (AT) refer to a sandbox of methods and tools to enable and
to govern the interactions of intelligent software agents, so as to shape their autonomy
and help them reach agreements that are acceptable to all stakeholders. In open
multiagent systems, and AI systems in general, autonomy should be exercised in a
responsible manner [13] so that decisions and behaviour obey ethical principles and
human values. This requirement has been referred to asvalue alignment[19, 64] of
(distributed) AI systems. In recent years, efforts to engineer value-aligned AI systems
led to proposals implementing the notion ofvalue-awarenessin autonomous agents [47,
70], where agents are endowed with explicit representations of human values and the
ability to reason with and about them.
Once there is an agreement on the meaning of a particular value in a specific
domain, and a computational way to express the level of alignment of entities with that
value (either quantitatively or in terms of qualitative preferences), different types of
reasoning can be performed in systems of value-aware agents. Several proposals have
been put forward that dynamically achieve value alignment by defining value-based
2

agent decision-making strategies [25–27, 58, 61], selecting different system configura-
tions (i.e. norms) [46, 67], or aggregating value-based preferences (sometimes called
value systems) [38, 39, 43]. However, such computational representations of values are
notoriously difficult to engineer.
Russell [64] synthesises three ambitious principles for designing truly generally
value-aligned machines. They should not only (1) maximize the realization of human
preferences, and (2) know how the preferences are defined, but (3) should also be
able to learn them from human behaviour. Some recent works follow this idea [22,
57] by mimicking agent behaviour using different forms of imitation. However, such
approaches are often limited by the fact that learned behaviours cannot be explained
in terms of the underlying ethical principles.

id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04518v1
published: 2026-02-04T13:07:15Z
summary: Agreement Technologies refer to open computer systems in which autonomous software agents interact with one another, typically on behalf of humans, in order to come to mutually acceptable agreements. With the advance of AI systems in recent years, it has become apparent that such agreements, in order to be acceptable to the involved parties, must remain aligned with ethical principles and moral values. However, this is notoriously difficult to ensure, especially as different human users (and their software agents) may hold different value systems, i.e. they may differently weigh the importance of individual moral values. Furthermore, it is often hard to specify the precise meaning of a value in a particular context in a computational manner. Methods to estimate value systems based on human-engineered specifications, e.g. based on value surveys, are limited in scale due to the need for intense human moderation. In this article, we propose a novel method to automatically \emph{learn} value systems from observations and human demonstrations. In particular, we propose a formal model of the \emph{value system learning} problem, its instantiation to sequential decision-making domains based on multi-objective Markov decision processes, as well as tailored preference-based and inverse reinforcement learning algorithms to infer value grounding functions and value systems. The approach is illustrated and evaluated by two simulated use cases.

title: Distributed Safety Critical Control among Uncontrollable Agents Using Reconstructed Control Barrier Functions
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10836v4
published: 2026-03-11T14:41:48Z
summary: This paper investigates the distributed safety critical control for multi-agent systems (MASs) in the presence of uncontrollable agents with uncertain behaviors. To ensure system safety, the control barrier function (CBF) is employed in this paper. However, a key challenge is that the CBF constraints are coupled when MASs perform collaborative tasks, which depend on information from multiple agents and impede the design of a fully distributed safe control scheme. To overcome this, a novel reconstructed CBF approach is proposed. In this method, the coupled CBF is reconstructed by leveraging state estimates of other agents obtained from a distributed adaptive observer. Furthermore, a prescribed performance adaptive parameter is designed to modify this reconstruction, ensuring that satisfying the reconstructed CBF constraint is sufficient to meet the original coupled one. Based on the reconstructed CBF, we design a safety-critical quadratic programming (QP) controller and prove that the proposed distributed control scheme rigorously guarantees the safety of the MAS, even in the uncertain dynamic environments involving uncontrollable agents. The effectiveness of the proposed method is illustrated through a simulation.

title: AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02841v2
published: 2025-10-01T08:10:37Z
summary: A fundamental limitation of current LLM-based AI agents is their inability to build differentiated trust among each other at the onset of an agent-to-agent dialogue. However, autonomous and interoperable trust establishment becomes essential once agents start to operate beyond isolated environments and engage in dialogues across individual or organizational boundaries. A promising way to fill this gap in Agentic AI is to equip agents with long-lived digital identities and introduce tamper-proof and flexible identity-bound attestations of agents, provisioned by commonly trusted third parties and designed for cross-domain verifiability. This article presents a conceptual framework and a prototypical multi-agent system, where each agent is endowed with a self-sovereign digital identity. It combines a unique and ledger-anchored W3C Decentralized Identifier (DID) of an agent with a set of third-party issued W3C Verifiable Credentials (VCs). This enables agents at the start of a dialog to prove ownership of their self-controlled DIDs for authentication purposes and to establish various cross-domain trust relationships through the spontaneous exchange of their self-hosted DID-bound VCs. A comprehensive evaluation of the prototypical implementation demonstrates technical feasibility but also reveals limitations once an agent's LLM is in sole charge to control the respective security procedures.

title: Establishing Shared Query Understanding in an Open Multi-Agent System
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2305.09349v1
published: 2023-05-16T11:07:05Z
summary: We propose a method that allows to develop shared understanding between two agents for the purpose of performing a task that requires cooperation. Our method focuses on efficiently establishing successful task-oriented communication in an open multi-agent system, where the agents do not know anything about each other and can only communicate via grounded interaction. The method aims to assist researchers that work on human-machine interaction or scenarios that require a human-in-the-loop, by defining interaction restrictions and efficiency metrics. To that end, we point out the challenges and limitations of such a (diverse) setup, while also restrictions and requirements which aim to ensure that high task performance truthfully reflects the extent to which the agents correctly understand each other.
